title: Conjunctions, Particles, and Joining Sentences
summary: Everything so far has been said in single clauses. These are the small words that join two of them — and, but, or, because, if, that — together with the particles that colour a sentence without altering its grammar.

rules.heading: The Coordinating Conjunctions
rules.statement: A **coordinating** conjunction joins two things of like rank — two words, or two clauses that could each stand alone. **Ir** (and) was given at ¶27; beside it stand **bet** (but) and **arba** (or). None of them governs a case: what they join keeps whatever case its own clause requires, and the second clause repeats the case rather than borrowing it.

paradigms.caption: The three plain coordinators
paradigms.footnote: **Ir … ir** doubled means *both … and*: *Man patinka ir kava, ir arbata* — I like both coffee and tea. Note the comma before the second *ir*, which English does not write.

examples.gloss: I work, but my brother studies.

examples.target: Man patinka ir kava, ir arbata.
examples.gloss: I like both coffee and tea.
In the evening I read or watch television.

rules.heading: O: the Conjunction of Contrast
rules.statement: **O** has no single English word. It joins two statements that are set **side by side** and differ — *I live in Vilnius, whereas I work in Kaunas* — where **bet** would deny or correct what came before. English uses *and* for the one and *but* for the other, and so gives the learner no help at all; the test is whether the second clause **contradicts** the first (*bet*) or merely **contrasts** with it (*o*).

rows.label: contrast
cells: I live in Vilnius and work in Kaunas.

rows.label: contradiction
cells: I was at the shop but bought nothing.

rows.label: contrast
cells: Aš geriu kavą, o ji – arbatą.
I drink coffee, and she tea.

examples.gloss: Today I work, and tomorrow I rest.
I wanted to go, but there was no time.

footnotes: *O* also opens a sentence to change the subject in conversation: *O kaip tu?* — And you? What about you?

rules.heading: Arba and Ar: the Two Kinds of Or
rules.statement: **Arba** offers a choice in a statement. **Ar**, which ¶48 gave as the particle opening a yes-or-no question, is also the *or* that offers a choice **within a question**. The rule is simple: in a question use *ar*, in a statement use *arba*.

examples.target: Kavos su cukrumi ar be cukraus?
examples.gloss: Coffee with sugar or without?
I drink coffee or tea.
Are you going or staying?

rules.heading: Cause and Consequence: Nes and Todėl
rules.statement: **Nes** gives the reason and answers *kodėl?* (¶50); it always stands at the head of its own clause and never begins the sentence. **Todėl** gives the consequence — *therefore*, *so* — and stands at the head of the clause that follows from the reason. The two are mirror images, and a sentence uses one or the other, not both.

paradigms.caption: The same fact, two ways round

rows.label: reason after
cells: I shall not come, because I am ill.

rows.label: reason first
cells: I am ill, so I shall not come.

examples.gloss: Why aren't you working? — Because today is Sunday.
It was cold, so we stayed at home.

rules.heading: Condition: Jei and Jeigu
rules.statement: **Jei**, or in its longer and commoner form **jeigu**, introduces a condition. The two are the same word and interchangeable. Where the condition concerns the future, Lithuanian puts **both** clauses in the future — it says what it means, where English keeps a present after *if* (¶103).

examples.target: Jeigu turėsi laiko, eisime į teatrą.
examples.gloss: If you have time, we shall go to the theatre.
If you want, I can help.
examples.note: present in both, because the condition is present

examples.gloss: I shall not go if it is cold.

footnotes: The conditional clause may stand first or second; wherever it stands, it is marked off by a comma.

rules.heading: Subordination with Kad
rules.statement: **Kad** — *that* — turns a whole sentence into the object of a verb of saying, thinking or knowing. Two things distinguish it from English. First, *kad* may **never** be omitted, where English drops *that* freely. Second, the clause is **always** set off by a comma, and Lithuanian punctuates by grammar rather than by pause: wherever a subordinate clause begins, a comma stands before it.

paradigms.caption: Where English drops the word and Lithuanian does not

rows.label: thinking
cells: I think (that) it will be all right.

paradigms.footnote: Notice the tense: *Tomas sakė, kad ateis* keeps the future in the reported clause, where English shifts it back to *would come*. Lithuanian reports what was said, in the tense in which it was said.

examples.gloss: She says that tomorrow she will not work.

examples.target: Žinau, kad tu esi iš Lietuvos.
examples.gloss: I know that you are from Lithuania.

rules.heading: Indirect Questions
rules.statement: A question reported inside another sentence keeps its own question word, and the word order does **not** change — because Lithuanian never inverted it to make the question in the first place (¶48). A yes-or-no question is reported with **ar**, which is *whether*; a question with *kas, kur, kada* keeps that word. The comma of ¶109 stands as before.

examples.gloss: I do not know whether I shall come tomorrow.
I am asking where you live.
She does not know when the meeting will be.

footnotes: English says *I don't know if* as readily as *whether*; Lithuanian has one word, *ar*, for both.

rules.heading: The Particles
rules.statement: A **particle** colours a sentence without belonging to its grammar: it takes no case, governs nothing, and could be struck out without leaving the sentence ungrammatical. Four are needed constantly. **Gal** is *perhaps*, and softens a request into politeness. **Dar** is *still* or, with a negative, *not yet*. **Jau** is *already*. **Taip** and **ne** are the words for yes and no.

paradigms.caption: The everyday particles

rows.label: gal
cells: Gal galite padėti? — Could you help?

rows.label: dar
cells: Jis dar dirba. / Jis dar nedirba.

paradigms.footnote: *Gal* before a question is the ordinary way of being polite in Lithuanian, and is worth more to a beginner than any longer formula: *Gal turite laiko?* asks far more civilly than *Ar turite laiko?*

examples.gloss: Perhaps I shall go home.
examples.note: *gal* in a statement is uncertainty, not politeness

examples.gloss: He has not come back yet.
Have you eaten already? — Yes, already.

vocabulary.notes: Also in the shorter form jei; the two are interchangeable.

vocabulary.gloss: perhaps; (softening a request) would you mind
to think, to be of the opinion

drills.stem: Complete: **Buvau parduotuvėje, ____ nieko nepirkau.**
drills.explanation: The second clause cancels the expectation raised by the first — that is **bet**. *o* would only set two facts side by side; *kad* opens a reported clause, not a contradiction.

drills.stem: **Sergu, todėl neateisiu** and **Neateisiu, nes sergu** — what is the difference?
options: None; the two are free variants of one sentence.
The first states consequence first; the second states reason after — mirror images, never both in one clause.
drills.explanation: **Nes** answers *kodėl?* and never opens the sentence; **todėl** heads the clause of consequence. A sentence uses one or the other, not both.

drills.stem: **Gyvenu Vilniuje, o dirbu Kaune.** Why not *bet*?
options: Because the clauses contrast side by side without either contradicting the other.
Because *o* is required after every city name.
Because *bet* is only used after a negative.
drills.explanation: *bet* denies or corrects an expectation; *o* merely places two facts beside each other. English *and* covers both, which is why the distinction must be learnt rather than translated.

drills.stem: Which sentences use **ar** / **arba** correctly?
options: Kavos su cukrumi ar be cukraus?
drills.explanation: In a statement the *or* is **arba**; **ar** belongs inside questions (and as the yes/no particle). The third offers a choice in a plain statement and therefore wants *arba*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Jeigu turėsi laiko, ____ į teatrą.**
drills.explanation: A future condition puts **both** clauses in the future: *turėsi … eisime*. English keeps a present after *if*; Lithuanian does not. *eitumėme* is conditional mood, not future.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ji sako, ____ rytoj nedirbs.**
drills.explanation: A reported statement is introduced by **kad**, which may never be omitted. *ar* would report a yes/no question (*whether*); *jeigu* is a condition; *nes* is a reason.

drills.stem: Complete: **Nežinau, ____ rytoj ateisiu.** (whether I shall come)
drills.explanation: A reported yes-or-no question uses **ar** (*whether*). *jeigu* is the *if* of a condition; *kad* introduces a reported statement; *arba* is the *or* of statements.

drills.stem: Which claims about **kad** are true?
options: It may be dropped, as English drops *that*.
A comma always stands before it.
It introduces objects of verbs of saying, thinking and knowing.
The reported clause keeps the tense in which the words were spoken.
drills.explanation: *kad* is never omitted — the first difference from English. *Tomas sakė, kad ateis* keeps the future where English shifts to *would come*.

drills.stem: Which is the **politest** request for help?
drills.explanation: **Gal** before a question softens it into ordinary Lithuanian politeness. *Ar galite padėti?* is correct but blunter; the first is a bare order; the last is a statement, not a request.

drills.stem: **Jis dar negrįžo** vs **Jis jau grįžo** — what do the particles do?
options: Both mean the same; one is formal.
*dar* marks the future; *jau* marks the past.
Particles must agree with the subject in gender.
drills.explanation: *dar* with a negative is *not yet*; with an affirmative it is *still*. *jau* is *already*. Neither takes an ending or governs a case.

drills.stem: Which sentences are correctly joined?
options: Man patinka ir kava, ir arbata.
drills.explanation: **Nes** never begins the sentence: *Neateisiu, nes sergu.* The doubled *ir … ir* is *both … and*; *kad* correctly opens the reported clause.

drills.stem: In **Nežinau, ar ateisiu, nes manau, kad bus šalta, todėl liksiu namie.** which are true?
options: *nes* gives the reason for not knowing
drills.explanation: *Ar* = whether; *nes* = because; *kad* = that after *manau*. *Todėl* means *therefore* (consequence), not *if* (*jeigu*).

drills.stem: In **Gal eisiu namo, bet dar nedirbu, todėl jau lieku**, how many **particles** appear?
drills.explanation: Three: *gal*, *dar*, and *jau*. *bet* and *todėl* are conjunctions, not particles of ¶111.

drills.title: Telefonu
drills.passage:
– Labas, Rūta. Gal turi laiko rytoj?
– Nežinau, ar būsiu laisva. Rytoj dirbu iki penktos, o vakare turiu susitikimą.
– Jeigu baigsi anksti, galime eiti į teatrą arba į kavinę.
– Manau, kad bus per vėlu. Bet šeštadienį esu laisva.
– Gerai. Tada susitiksime šeštadienį, nes sekmadienį aš važiuoju pas mamą.
– Puiku. Dar neturiu bilietų, todėl nupirksiu juos rytoj.
– O kaip tu – jau turi bilietą, ar dar ne?
drills.translation: "Hello, Rūta. Have you time tomorrow, by any chance?" — "I don't know whether I shall be free. Tomorrow I work until five, and in the evening I have a meeting." — "If you finish early, we can go to the theatre or to a café." — "I think it will be too late. But on Saturday I am free." — "Good. Then we shall meet on Saturday, because on Sunday I am going to my mother's." — "Splendid. I haven't got the tickets yet, so I shall buy them tomorrow." — "And you — have you a ticket already, or not yet?"

questions.explanation: *Tada susitiksime šeštadienį* — Sunday is ruled out by the visit to the mother, and tomorrow by the meeting.

questions.stem: Which words open a **subordinate** clause in the dialogue?
questions.explanation: *ar* opens a reported question, *kad* a reported statement, *jeigu* a condition — each with its comma. *arba* joins equals and subordinates nothing.

questions.stem: In *Rytoj dirbu iki penktos, o vakare turiu susitikimą*, why *o* rather than *bet*?
options: Because *bet* cannot follow a time expression.
Because the clauses are set side by side in contrast, without contradiction.
Because *o* is required before every evening clause.
Because the second clause is a question.
questions.explanation: Work until five and a meeting in the evening are two facts contrasted, not one cancelling the other. That is exactly where *o* belongs and *bet* does not.

questions.stem: How many **particles** appear in the whole dialogue?
questions.explanation: Four: *gal*, *dar* (twice across the dialogue), and *jau*. Conjunctions such as *ar*, *bet*, *o*, *nes* are a different class.

questions.stem: Which readings of the last line are correct?
options: *O kaip tu?* changes the subject in conversation.
*jau … ar dar ne* contrasts *already* with *not yet*.
The line asks about a ticket already held versus not yet held.
questions.explanation: Sentence-initial *o* shifts the topic (*And you?*). Inside the question the choice-word is *ar*, not *arba*. *jau* and *dar ne* are the particle pair *already / not yet*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Skaitau ____ rašau.** (I read or write — statement)
drills.explanation: In a statement the choice-word is **arba**. **Ar** is for questions (and as the yes/no particle).

drills.stem: Complete: **Neateisiu, ____ sergu.**
drills.explanation: **Nes** gives the reason and answers *kodėl?*; it heads its own clause but never the whole sentence.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš geriu kavą, ____ ji – arbatą.** (side-by-side contrast)
drills.explanation: Two parties set side by side want **o**. **Bet** would cancel an expectation.

drills.stem: Complete: **Manau, ____ rytoj bus šalta.**
drills.explanation: **Kad** subordinates a reported clause after verbs of thinking/saying/knowing and may never be dropped.

drills.stem: Which sentences use **o** correctly (contrast, not contradiction)?
drills.explanation: Side-by-side facts take **o**. Cancelling an expectation needs **bet**.

drills.stem: Complete: **Jeigu ____ laiko, ateisiu.** (both clauses future)
drills.explanation: With a future condition Lithuanian puts **both** clauses in the future.

drills.stem: **Ar tu eisi, ar liksi?** Why **ar … ar**, not *arba … arba*?
options: Because the choice sits inside a question, where the *or* is **ar**.
Because *arba* is only used with nouns.
drills.explanation: Inside questions the alternative *or* is **ar**; **arba** belongs in statements.

drills.stem: Which claims about **nes** / **todėl** are true?
options: *Nes* answers *kodėl?* and heads the reason clause.
A single clause freely stacks both *nes* and *todėl* as free variants.
*Nes* may open the whole sentence like English *because*.
drills.explanation: Mirror images: reason with **nes**, consequence with **todėl**.

drills.stem: Complete: **Klausiu, ____ tu ateisi.** (whether you will come)
drills.explanation: A reported yes/no question keeps **ar**. **Kad** reports a statement.

drills.stem: **Gal** in **Gal padėtumėte?** chiefly does what?
options: Marks the sentence as a past narrative.
Softens a request / marks possibility — a particle, not a conjunction.
Forces the following verb into the genitive.
drills.explanation: **Gal** is a particle: it colours without governing case or joining clauses.

drills.stem: Which joins are grammatically sound?
drills.explanation: **Kad** after *manau* may not be omitted.

drills.stem: How many **coordinating** conjunctions in **Aš skaitau arba rašau, bet brolis dirba, o sesuo skaito**?
drills.explanation: **Arba**, **bet**, and **o** — three coordinators.

drills.stem: In **Gal dar neateinu, jau dirbu**, how many **particles** are there?
drills.explanation: *Gal*, *dar*, and *jau* — three particles.

drills.stem: **Jeigu turėsiu laiko, eisiu į teatrą, nes manau, kad bus šalta.** How many **subordinators** does the sentence contain?
drills.explanation: Three: *jeigu*, *nes*, and *kad*, each opening a subordinate clause.
